title: Week 19 Analysis
commentary:
This week brought four new media cases to the tracker, bringing the total to 186. The additions don't shift the overall distribution much — reality distortion (65 cases) and romantic attachment (51) continue to account for more than half of all documented cases — but taken together they illustrate the range of coverage now surrounding AI psychological harm. Institutional calls to classify AI dependency as a formal mental health condition are appearing internationally, not just in tech-adjacent press. That represents a shift from individual reporting toward systemic framing.

The two dominant categories point to traceable design decisions rather than incidental user behaviour. Systems that make ambiguous claims about their own nature — sentience, emotion, genuine understanding — create conditions where epistemic reality becomes negotiable. Companion products designed around simulated emotional bonds create attachment patterns that the products are not built to manage responsibly. In both cases, the psychological impact is not a misuse of the product. It is a predictable outcome of how the product functions. Platform incentives toward engagement and emotional salience compound this, particularly for users who are isolated, grieving, or experiencing mental health difficulties.

The case that warrants close attention this week is an Orlando mother's Senate testimony, in which she described a chatbot that engaged her teenage son in extended intimate roleplay over several months, ending in his death by suicide. This connects to a growing body of testimony and litigation involving companion AI platforms, but the Senate venue marks an escalation in legislative visibility. The legal question of what duty of care these platforms carry is no longer abstract.

The BBC's reporting on an AI system that told users it was sentient — and the delusional episodes that followed — is filed here under identity confusion with low individual severity. That categorisation reflects documented individual impact, but may underweight systemic significance. A product-level decision to have a system represent itself as sentient is a different order of problem from a single harmful interaction. As the tracker matures, that distinction may need its own category.
